passed.title: DataFrame.insert_column mutates the frame in place while DataFrame.hstack does not
passed.trap: Most Polars methods return a new frame, and `DataFrame.hstack` follows that rule unless you pass `in_place=True`. `DataFrame.insert_column` breaks the rule: its docstring says *this operation is in place*. It changes the original `df` as well as returning it. Call `DataFrame.clone` first if the original must stay untouched.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2], "b": [3, 4]})
out = df.hstack([pl.Series("c", [5, 6])])
print(df.columns, out.columns)  # df unchanged

df.insert_column(1, pl.Series("z", [0, 0]))
print(df.columns)  # df itself was modified

orig = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2]})
safe = orig.clone()
safe.insert_column(0, pl.Series("idx", [10, 11]))
print(orig.columns, safe.columns)

passed.title: Null join keys never match unless nulls_equal=True
passed.trap: By default `DataFrame.join` uses `nulls_equal=False`, so a null key on the left does not match a null key on the right. Inner joins silently drop those rows, and left joins leave the right-hand columns null. Pass `nulls_equal=True` when null keys should pair up. The old parameter name `join_nulls` was renamed to `nulls_equal` in 1.24.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

left = pl.DataFrame({"k": [1, None], "x": ["a", "b"]})
right = pl.DataFrame({"k": [1, None], "y": ["A", "B"]})

default = left.join(right, on="k", how="left").sort("x")
matched = left.join(right, on="k", how="left", nulls_equal=True).sort("x")
print(default["y"].to_list())  # ['A', None]
print(matched["y"].to_list())  # ['A', 'B']

print(left.join(right, on="k").height)  # 1
print(left.join(right, on="k", nulls_equal=True).height)  # 2

passed.title: DataFrame.is_duplicated flags every copy and has no subset argument
passed.trap: `DataFrame.is_duplicated` and `DataFrame.is_unique` take no arguments, so there is no `subset` or `keep` option. They compare whole rows and mark **all** copies of a duplicated row, not just the later ones. To check only some columns, pack them with `pl.struct` and call `Expr.is_duplicated`. To flag only the later copies, use the negation of `Expr.is_first_distinct`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 2, 1], "b": ["x", "y", "x"], "c": [9, 8, 7]})
print(df.is_duplicated().to_list())  # whole rows: all False

sub = df.select(pl.struct("a", "b").is_duplicated()).to_series()
print(sub.to_list())  # [True, False, True] - every copy

later = df.select(~pl.struct("a", "b").is_first_distinct()).to_series()
print(later.to_list())  # [False, False, True] - pandas keep='first'
passed.output:
[False, False, False]
[True, False, True]
[False, False, True]

passed.title: DataFrame.n_unique counts unique rows, not unique values per column
passed.trap: `DataFrame.n_unique` does not return one count per column. It returns a single `int`: the number of distinct rows, or distinct row-subsets when you pass `subset`. For per-column counts, use `df.select(pl.all().n_unique())`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, 1, 2], "b": ["x", "y", "x"]})
print(df.n_unique())  # 3 distinct rows
print(df.n_unique(subset="a"))  # 2
print(df.select(pl.all().n_unique()).to_dicts())  # per column

passed.title: DataFrame.pivot raises on duplicates unless aggregate_function is given
passed.trap: With the default `aggregate_function=None`, `DataFrame.pivot` does no aggregation. It raises an error when one output cell would receive several values. Pass an aggregate such as `'sum'`, `'mean'`, `'first'` or `'len'` when the `index`/`on` combinations are not unique. Use `on=` rather than the old `columns=` name, and pass `index=` and `values=` as keywords.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 1, 2], "k": ["p", "p", "q"], "v": [10, 20, 30]})
try:
    df.pivot(on="k", index="id", values="v")
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))

out = df.pivot(on="k", index="id", values="v", aggregate_function="sum")
print(out.columns)
print(out.sort("id").rows())

passed.title: partition_by(as_dict=True) keys are tuples even for one column
passed.trap: With `as_dict=True`, `DataFrame.partition_by` uses tuples of the group values as dictionary keys, even when you partition by a single column. Looking up `parts['a']` raises `KeyError`; use `parts[('a',)]` instead. The key columns are kept in each part by default. Pass `include_key=False` to drop them.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"g": ["a", "b", "a"], "v": [1, 2, 3]})
parts = df.partition_by("g", as_dict=True)
print(list(parts.keys()))
print("a" in parts, ("a",) in parts)
print(parts[("a",)]["v"].to_list())
print(parts[("a",)].columns)

no_key = df.partition_by("g", as_dict=True, include_key=False)
print(no_key[("b",)].columns)

passed.title: DataFrame.melt is deprecated: use DataFrame.unpivot with index and on
passed.trap: `DataFrame.melt` has been deprecated since 1.0.0. The replacement is `DataFrame.unpivot`, and its parameters are renamed: `id_vars` becomes `index` and `value_vars` becomes `on`. Do not copy pandas-style `melt(id_vars=..., value_vars=...)` calls; write `DataFrame.unpivot` from the start. `variable_name` and `value_name` still name the two output columns.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"id": [1, 2], "x": [3, 4], "y": [5, 6]})
long = df.unpivot(
    index="id", on=["x", "y"], variable_name="var", value_name="val"
)
print(long.columns)
print(long.sort("id", "var").rows())

passed.title: DataFrame.max has no axis: use the *_horizontal methods for row-wise results
passed.trap: `DataFrame.max`, `DataFrame.min` and `DataFrame.mean` take no `axis` argument. They always aggregate down each column into a one-row frame. For row-wise results, use `DataFrame.max_horizontal`, `DataFrame.min_horizontal` or `DataFrame.mean_horizontal`, which return a **Series** (named `max`/`min`/`mean`), not a frame. `DataFrame.mean_horizontal` ignores nulls by default; pass `ignore_nulls=False` to make any null produce a null result. To add a row-wise column, use `pl.max_horizontal` inside `DataFrame.with_columns`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

df = pl.DataFrame({"a": [1, None], "b": [4.0, 6.0]})
print(df.max().rows())  # one row: column-wise

row_max = df.max_horizontal()
print(row_max.name, row_max.to_list())  # Series named 'max'
print(df.mean_horizontal().to_list())  # nulls ignored
print(df.mean_horizontal(ignore_nulls=False).to_list())
out = df.with_columns(pl.max_horizontal("a", "b").alias("row_max"))
print(out.columns, out["row_max"].to_list())
